findings.title: limitFunction drops all call arguments before invoking the wrapped function
findings.cause: The returned wrapper is zero-argument and calls function_() instead of forwarding ...arguments_ into the wrapped function.
findings.impact: Any consumer using limitFunction with a parameterized function receives undefined arguments at runtime despite the public type returning (...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>. This silently corrupts real workloads such as keyed fetches or writes.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-124 returns () => limit(() => function_()). index.d.ts:133-136 declares the returned function accepts the original Arguments. git show HEAD:index.js:117-120 forwarded (...arguments_) to function_(...arguments_).
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const fn = limitFunction((a, b) => [a, b], {concurrency: 1}); console.log(JSON.stringify(await fn('x', 'y')));" prints [null,null] instead of ["x","y"].

findings.title: limit.map omits the mapper index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call now passes iterableIsArray ? index : undefined, so Set, Map, generator, and iterator inputs no longer receive the Array.from index.
findings.impact: The documented iterable API is wrong for non-arrays. Consumers batching Sets or iterator results cannot rely on mapperFunction(value, index), causing wrong ordering keys, progress labels, or derived output.
findings.evidence: index.js:107-112 computes iterableIsArray and substitutes undefined for the index unless the input is an Array. readme.md:78-84 and index.d.ts:30-43 both state the mapper receives item value and index and is equivalent to Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)). git show HEAD:index.js:106-110 passed index unconditionally.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit(1); const seen = []; await limit.map(new Set(['a','b']), (value, index) => { seen.push([value, index]); return value; }); console.log(JSON.stringify(seen));" prints [["a",null],["b",null]] because undefined is serialized as null.

findings.title: Options object silently changes rejectOnClear default to true
findings.cause: The options destructuring defaults rejectOnClear to true when an options object omits it.
findings.impact: pLimit({concurrency: 1}) no longer behaves like pLimit(1). Calling clearQueue() unexpectedly rejects pending promises with AbortError, violating the documented default false and creating production-visible rejections in callers that only opted into object-form concurrency.
findings.evidence: index.js:6-8 destructures ({concurrency, rejectOnClear = true}). readme.md:46-52 and readme.md:149-155 document Default: false. index.d.ts:99-106 also documents Default: false. git show HEAD:index.js:4-8 defaulted rejectOnClear to false.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const first = limit(() => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 20))); const second = limit(() => 'never'); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); console.log(await Promise.race([second.then(() => 'resolved', error => error.name), new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve('still-pending'), 80))])); await first;" prints AbortError; with the documented default it should remain still-pending after clearQueue().

findings.title: rejectOnClear runtime validation accepts falsey non-booleans
findings.cause: Validation is guarded by rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== "boolean", so falsey invalid values bypass the type check.
findings.impact: JavaScript callers can pass invalid configuration such as 0, an empty string, or null and get silent behavior instead of the promised TypeError. This weakens input validation for config-driven consumers and contradicts the TypeScript test that rejects non-boolean rejectOnClear.
findings.evidence: index.js:12-14 only throws for truthy non-booleans. index.test-d.ts:28-29 expects rejectOnClear: "nope" to be rejected at type level, and the runtime error text says Expected `rejectOnClear` to be a boolean. git show HEAD:index.js:10-13 checked typeof rejectOnClear !== "boolean" without the truthiness guard.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [0, '', null]) { try { pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value}); console.log(String(value) + ':accepted'); } catch { console.log(String(value) + ':threw'); } }" prints accepted for all three invalid values.

findings.title: Infinity is no longer accepted as an unlimited concurrency value
findings.cause: validateConcurrency now requires Number.isInteger(concurrency), removing the prior Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY allowance used by both constructor and setter validation.
findings.impact: Consumers that disable limiting by passing Infinity or by setting limit.concurrency = Infinity now get a TypeError. This is an edge-case behavioral regression in a dependency API where Infinity is a common sentinel for unbounded concurrency.
findings.evidence: index.js:127-130 rejects any non-integer even when concurrency is Infinity. git show HEAD:index.js:123-126 accepted Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY when greater than zero. The same validateConcurrency function is used by pLimit(...) and the concurrency setter at index.js:94-96.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { pLimit(Infinity); console.log('constructor:accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log('constructor:threw', error.message); } const limit = pLimit(1); try { limit.concurrency = Infinity; console.log('setter:accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log('setter:threw', error.message); }" reports throws for both paths.
